section: 2. Monthly species time series (the grain at which phi is defined)
grain_in: one row per haul x species
grain_out: one row per stratum x month x species
units_out: counts (individuals) summed over the hauls in that stratum-month
operation: Sums haul level abundance to a monthly total per stratum, date and species, then numbers strata with sid and months within stratum with mo = as.integer(factor(date)), which orders by the character sort of the Date and so is chronological. The strata_key join and the mo index are absorbed: they only carry labels forward. The abundance is a raw sum over hauls, not a rate per haul, so it inherits any difference in the number of hauls per month. The assertion checks the number of distinct mo values over the whole table, which is 9 when at least one stratum has 9 months and none has more; a stratum with fewer than 9 months would pass unnoticed and would later give a shorter series to var and sd.
settings: stopifnot(n_months == 9), the 9 being three months per season times three years per period; month ordering taken from factor(date) level order
na_behavior: Sums are taken without na.rm, so any NA abund would propagate to the monthly total; abund is zero filled upstream so no NA is expected, which also means a genuinely unsampled month is represented as a real zero rather than as missing.

section: 2. Monthly species time series (the grain at which phi is defined)
grain_in: one row per stratum x month x species
grain_out: one row per active species x stratum, nine month columns
operation: Drops species x stratum series that are zero in every month, spreads the survivors into a species-stratum by month matrix with zero fill, and stores it as the numeric matrix X with sid_vec recording each row's stratum. The filter is on the group total, so it removes whole series rather than individual months. The pivot and the matrix extraction are absorbed as reshape. The comment justifies the filter as removing species that are inert in Eq. 6; they would contribute zero to var_C and zero to sum_sd_i, so this is a shortcut rather than a change of definition, and it does change the species count per stratum if that count is reported anywhere.
settings: filter(sum(abund_date) > 0) within sid and species_code; values_fill = 0; column selection as.character(seq_len(n_months)) assumes months are named 1 through 9
na_behavior: A species x stratum series that is missing entirely from sp_monthly is absent rather than zero, and is indistinguishable in X from one that was present but never caught, since both are simply not rows.

grain_in: one row per active species x stratum, nine month columns
grain_out: one row per stratum
units_out: sum_sd_i in counts, mu_C in counts per month, shannon an index
operation: Computes each species-stratum series standard deviation across the nine months, sums those within a stratum to get sum_sd_i, joins the Shannon index from the alpha diversity file, and computes mu_C as the stratum total over all species and months divided by nine, that is the mean community total per month. The arithmetic combining a quantity derived from X with a quantity read from a separate file is what makes this a node rather than a reshape. major_area and season are recast as factors for the mixed models. The header comment asserts that both quantities are invariant to the permutation, which holds because a within-row permutation preserves each row's multiset of values exactly.
settings: sd is the sample standard deviation with n-1 denominator; mu_C divisor is n_months = 9, not the number of months actually present; join to alpha_div on major_area, period and season where period is a factor on one side and read from CSV on the other, so the types must be checked

section: 4. Helpers: permutation, metric assembly, SEM fitting
grain_in: one row per active species x stratum, nine month columns
grain_out: same, with each row's months reordered independently
operation: Function definition. Permutes each species-stratum monthly series independently across the nine months by drawing uniforms, ordering them within row blocks and reindexing X, then rebuilding the matrix by row. The three index vectors immediately above (grp_cm, col_cm and row_rm) are part of this region but each carries a trailing comment and so cannot serve as the anchor, which is why the region is anchored at the function line; the region's true first statement is grp_cm <- rep(seq_len(N_rows), times = n_months). Because each row is permuted within itself, the row multiset is preserved exactly, so every species keeps its monthly mean, variance and total, and only the alignment of months between species is destroyed. Nothing is preserved about the community column totals.
settings: randomness from runif over N_rows * n_months values, drawn from the stream seeded at set.seed(2025); order() with a numeric key so exact ties are broken by position, which for continuous uniforms is a measure zero case; byrow = TRUE in the matrix rebuild, which must match the row-major index vectors
na_behavior: No missing handling. An NA anywhere in X would be permuted like any other value and would propagate into the metrics; X is built with zero fill so none is expected.

section: 4. Helpers: permutation, metric assembly, SEM fitting
grain_in: one row per species-stratum, nine month columns (matrix argument)
grain_out: one row per stratum
units_out: var_C in squared counts, I_C an invariability index, phi a unitless proportion in [0,1], plus their logs
operation: Function definition. Sums the species by month matrix within stratum to get community monthly totals, then computes the community variance across the nine months, invariability I_C as mu_C squared over var_C, synchrony phi as var_C over the square of sum_sd_i, and two log transforms. mu_C and sum_sd_i are taken from stratum_base and are not recomputed, which is what holds them fixed across permutations. The two logs use different bases: log10 for I_C and natural log for phi, so the two standardized slopes reported later are not on a common log scale, though standardization inside fit_std_sem removes the scale difference from the betas.
settings: guard var_C > 0 before dividing into mu_C squared; guard sum_sd_i > 0 before dividing into var_C; pmax(phi, 1e-6) floor applied before the log; var is the sample variance with n-1 denominator
na_behavior: I_C is NA when a stratum's community total is constant across months, and phi is NA when every species in a stratum has zero variance. Both collapse into the same NA, and downstream they are also indistinguishable from a stratum with missing shannon, because fit_std_sem filters all three columns in one step and reports no counts. Separately, the pmax floor turns a genuine phi of exactly 0 into log(1e-6), about -13.8, so a perfectly asynchronous stratum is retained as a finite and extreme value rather than dropped, and that value is set by the floor rather than by the data.

section: 4. Helpers: permutation, metric assembly, SEM fitting
grain_in: one row per stratum
grain_out: one row of two standardized slopes
units_in: index values and a diversity index
units_out: standardized regression coefficients, standard deviations per standard deviation
operation: Function definition and the call into nlme. Filters to strata where log_IC, log_phi and shannon are all finite, z-standardizes those three, and fits two linear mixed models: log_phi on shannon, and log_IC on shannon and log_phi, each with random intercepts specified as random = list(major_area = ~1, season = ~1). In nlme that list form specifies nested random effects, season within major_area, not crossed effects; if the intent was crossed area and season intercepts this does not fit that model. Both fits are wrapped in tryCatch and return the standardized shannon slope, so the returned stability coefficient is the direct effect of diversity on invariability with synchrony held in the model. Standardization happens after filtering and inside the function, so under permutation the scaling is recomputed on whichever strata survive that draw.
settings: REML estimation; lmeControl with optim, maxIter 200 and msMaxIter 200; na.action = na.omit; scale() uses the sample standard deviation; the random argument is a named list, which nlme reads as a nesting order rather than as crossed terms; only the shannon slope is returned, the log_phi slope in the second model is discarded
na_behavior: Any error in either fit returns NULL and then NA_real_. Non-convergence, a singular random effects structure, too few strata after filtering, and any other error all collapse into the same NA and cannot be told apart afterwards. Strata removed by the finite filter are not counted or reported, so a draw fitted on many fewer strata is indistinguishable from one fitted on all of them.

end_anchor: ci <- function(x) quantile(x, c(0.025, 0.975), na.rm = TRUE)
grain_in: one row per simulation, plus the two observed slopes
grain_out: two p-values and a percentile function
units_out: probabilities; interval bounds in coefficient units
operation: Extracts the two observed slopes, then forms one tailed permutation p-values with the (1 + r) / (1 + n) estimator, counting null stability slopes at or above the observed and null synchrony slopes at or below the observed. The two tests therefore run in opposite directions, each testing a signed prediction rather than a two sided departure, and the direction is embedded in the comparison operator rather than stated. The unname extractions at the top of the region only carry values forward and are absorbed, as is the quantile helper defined at the end, which supplies the interval reported next.
settings: one tailed: >= for stability, <= for synchrony; (1 + r) / (1 + n) estimator so the result can never be exactly 0 or 1; denominator counts non-NA simulations for that metric, so failed simulations shrink n rather than counting as non-exceedances; quantile at 0.025 and 0.975 using the default type 7 with na.rm = TRUE
na_behavior: NA null slopes are excluded from both numerator and denominator for their own metric, so the two p-values can rest on different numbers of simulations without that being visible. If the observed slope were NA, every comparison would be NA and na.rm = TRUE would give r = 0, producing the smallest attainable p-value rather than an error.
